Cathie Wood and 8 Other Big Funds Bought Airbnb Last Quarter. Ken Fisher and 11 Others Sold. Who's Right? ©Guillermo Spelucin, Andrea Davis from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the third quarter, nine bought Airbnb, including Cathie Wood's ARK Invest, and 12 sold, including Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments.

The sellers moved far more money, but two of the three biggest still own large Airbnb stakes, and Fisher sold only 1,600 shares.

Five of the buyers also sold or cut Palo Alto Networks, and the biggest buyer sold Booking Holdings and trimmed Expedia.

The buyers look right: at 27x forward earnings, near its five-year low, Airbnb can reach the Street's $206 target if today's estimates hold.

Big funds couldn't agree on Airbnb (ABNB:NASDAQ) last quarter.

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30 (funds investors know by name, or ones with $1 billion or more of US stocks in their 13Fs, leaving out quant and index funds), nine bought Airbnb. Each opened a position or added 20% or more to one. Twelve sold out or cut their stakes by 20% or more, and 28 held the stock at the quarter's end. Since Sept. 30, Airbnb is up 6%.

The buyers kept their bets small

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest added 48% to its stake, taking it to 218,989 shares, its 13F filed Nov. 13 shows. That's about $11 million of buying. The whole stake was worth $35 million at Sept. 30, just 0.2% of its 13F stocks for a firm that manages $17 billion. The biggest buyer was Meridiem Capital Partners, a $2.4 billion fund, which opened a 262,877-share position worth about $42 million, 1.8% of its 13F stocks. KR Capital, a $1.2 billion fund, raised its stake 169% to 91,405 shares. Larry Robbins' Glenview Capital and Lee Ainslie's Maverick Capital each opened stakes of about $2 million.

TIKR tracks 45 analysts on Airbnb. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Airbnb, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Airbnb's Analyst Ratings

The sellers moved far more money

Independent Franchise Partners, a $24 billion fund, cut its stake 20%, a sale worth about $178 million at quarter-end prices. That one cut is more than twice what all nine buyers added together. Yet it still held 4.32 million shares worth $693 million at Sept. 30, 4.3% of its 13F stocks. Consulta, a $3.1 billion fund (that's what its 13F holds in US stocks), cut its stake 29%. Airbnb is still its fifth-largest holding, at 7.8% of its 13F stocks.

The clean exit came from Akre Capital, a $12 billion fund, which sold all 1.18 million of its shares, about $169 million worth. Airbnb had been 3.3% of its 13F stocks a quarter earlier. Tom Gayner's Markel cut its stake 70%. And Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments, which manages $387 billion, sold all 1,600 of its shares. That's about $229,000, a rounding error for a firm that size.

title: Airbnb vs. DoorDash: Which Stock Is a Better Buy?
detail:
Airbnb vs. DoorDash: Which Stock Is a Better Buy?
Jack Delaney, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 12:45 PM MST 5 min read
ABNB
DASH
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors often weigh growth potential against current profitability when comparing Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) and DoorDash (NASDAQ:DASH). Both companies have transformed how consumers spend on experiences and daily conveniences, but their financial trajectories remain distinct.

Airbnb focuses on the global travel market by connecting hosts with guests seeking unique accommodations. DoorDash operates a local commerce platform that facilitates delivery from restaurants and retail merchants. While both benefit from digital shifts, their cost structures and capital requirements differ significantly.

Image source: Getty Images.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a two-sided global marketplace that connects more than 5 million hosts with guests across roughly 220 countries. The company focuses on expanding its brand through strategic partnerships with cultural and entertainment organizations to attract a diverse range of travelers. This positioning within consumer discretionary stocks allows it to capture spending on both short-term vacations and long-term stays.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $13.9 billion, representing growth of approximately 16.7% over the prior year. The company demonstrated significant bottom-line strength by generating a net income of close to $3.2 billion during this same period. This level of profitability is a hallmark of its asset-light business model, which avoids the costs of owning physical properties.

The case for DoorDash

DoorDash operates a local commerce platform that connects merchants, consumers, and delivery couriers across more than 40 countries. The company has evolved beyond restaurant delivery into grocery and convenience sectors, maintaining agreements with over 600,000 merchants. Growth is further supported by over 56 million monthly active users and a proposed $17 billion acquisition of Instacart to solidify its market position.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $17.1 billion, which is a significant 35% increase compared to the previous twelve-month period. The company also reached a milestone by reporting a net income of approximately $1.1 billion.

Risk profile comparison

Airbnb faces intense competition from established online travel agencies like Booking Holdings (NASDAQ:BKNG) and Expedia Group (NASDAQ:EXPE), as well as traditional hotel chains. The company is also subject to evolving legal and regulatory environments, particularly restrictive short-term rental laws in major markets like New York City. Additionally, reliance on third-party payment processors and other threats present ongoing operational risks.

NVDA

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) has historically posted strong growth metrics. This is usually what happens when businesses disrupt massive industries and quickly steal market share.

Momentum is picking up. During the third quarter (ended Sept. 30), the company reported a year-over-year revenue gain of 19%, beating analyst estimates. Gross booking value climbed 21%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Besides the growth story, investors shouldn't overlook Airbnb's impressive profitability. Trailing-12-month free cash flow (FCF) of $4.9 billion accounted for 35% of revenue, which is a superb margin. The board of directors had the confidence to approve a $12 billion buyback, in addition to the $2.7 billion in existing capacity.

The growth stock has had a wonderful year. It's up 33% in 2026 (as of Nov. 18). Here's what that share repurchase runway means for investors.

Image source: Getty Images.

A shrinking share count benefits long-term owners

Airbnb is known for having sizable stock-based compensation, totaling $1.4 billion over the last nine months. This is how businesses, particularly those earlier in their life cycles, pay their employees. But it results in an increase in the share count.

To Airbnb's credit, though, its outstanding share count shrank by almost 3% in the past year. The company conducted $4 billion in stock buybacks over the last 12 months. Combining the new $12 billion repurchase authorization with the $2.7 billion remaining capacity means Airbnb now intends to buy 12% of the company's entire market capitalization.

Investors benefit from this tailwind. A smaller outstanding share count provides a jolt to earnings per share (EPS). Shareholders who continue to hold the stock see their ownership percentage in the business increase over time.

The best companies can balance returning capital to investors with reinvesting into their operations. Airbnb is certainly still playing offense.

The business continues to expand its list of services. Travelers can now book hotels. And there are more active partnerships in place. And for hosts, a redesigned calendar makes juggling multiple listings far simpler.

Airbnb is also leaning into the opportunity that artificial intelligence (AI) presents. It plans to release an AI-powered travel assistant in 2027.

Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

Airbnb (ABNB) stock returned 53.2% over the past twelve months, against 11.0% for the S&P 500. After that rise, the question is what could lift the shares next. Airbnb is already large, taking nearly 0.5 million bookings a day. During its November 5, 2026 call, management named one business growing faster than its core business. What is that business, and how far along is Airbnb with it?

All of that 53.2% came from the share price, because Airbnb pays no dividend. Part of your money can pay you income while you wait for the next move. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, and it lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. See the metrics.

Airbnb Now Lists Thousands Of Hotels

The business is hotels. The platform now lists thousands of boutique and independent hotels across more than 60 top destinations. During the November 5 call, management said hotel bookings accelerated again in the third quarter of fiscal 2026. Hotels are also growing markedly faster than Airbnb's core business.

It is still early, though. Hotels are growing "off of a very, very tiny base," in management's words. Management said the hotel industry has also come round to Airbnb, after some animosity in the early 2010s. In its view, hotels now see it as a major ally, because it brings them an audience that is disproportionately Gen Z.

How Big Could Hotels Get For Airbnb?

Management called hotels a $900 billion market. It said Airbnb will make multiple billions of dollars in hotel revenue in the coming years.

To view that against the whole company, Airbnb recorded revenue of $13.9 billion over the twelve months to September 30, 2026. That was up 16.7%, following growth of 10.2% in the twelve months before. A few billion dollars from hotels would be a large addition to Airbnb, not a sideline.

Airbnb stock trades at 7.6 times sales, against 3.1 for the S&P 500. On November 18, the shares closed 5.4% below their highest close of the past year. Buyers at that price appear to assume the company keeps growing well ahead of the market, and hotels offer one place that growth could come from.

What Does Airbnb Still Have To Prove?

Airbnb still has to give a forecast for hotels. On the November 5 call, management declined to give any projection for the hotel business. Until it does, you cannot measure how much hotels add.

New businesses also cost money, and that shows in how much of each booking Airbnb keeps. The share of bookings Airbnb kept as revenue was 17.6% in the third quarter, down slightly from a year earlier. Management said that was mainly due to Reserve Now, Pay Later, which lets guests book now and pay closer to the stay. A smaller part came from incentives and credits for new business initiatives.

Will the future of growth be driven by global travel experiences or the expansion of independent digital commerce? Deciding between Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB)and Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP)involves choosing between two very different platform leaders.

Airbnb connects millions of travelers with unique stays, while Shopify provides the software backbone for modern retail. Both companies benefit from powerful network effects, where more users or merchants make the platform more valuable for everyone involved.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates as a massive marketplace for lodging and experiences, connecting more than 5 million hosts with guests in roughly 220 countries. In its latest annual report, the company highlights its reliance on Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) for platform hosting and its use of third-party providers for community support. As the platform evolves, it is exploring the use of AI in travel to enhance its search capabilities and host support.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $13.9 billion. This represents a revenue growth of approximately 16.7% compared to the prior twelve-month period. During the same time frame, the company reported net income of nearly $3.2 billion.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with liquid assets, reached roughly 1.4x. The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is approximately 0.3x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $4.6 billion, though note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.

The case for Shopify

Shopify serves as the central operating system for millions of merchants across 175 countries, providing tools for both online and in-store sales. The company supports everyone from small entrepreneurs to large enterprise brands, relying on partners like PayPal and Stripe for payment processing. This ecosystem approach allows it to scale without owning inventory, creating a software-centric business model with high recurring potential.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached close to $14.2 billion. This reflects a revenue growth of roughly 32.5% over the preceding period. Shopify also reported a net income of approximately $2.1 billion for these twelve months.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 6.0x, indicating a strong ability to meet short-term obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.0x, indicating a very low level of debt relative to equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $2.0 billion, and stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.
